Question 4 integrated into FR-072, FR-062, Edge Cases, and a new acceptance scenario.

## Question 5 of up to 5

**Question:** Should the stored form of a password be deliberately slow to compute, so that someone who obtains a copy of the storage directory cannot cheaply guess weak passwords, or is a fast salted one-way transformation sufficient? (FR-056)

**Why it matters:** FR-056 forbids storing a form "from which the password itself can be recovered" — but a fast salted hash of a weak password *is* recoverable by guessing, so the requirement's bar is currently ambiguous and the Assumptions section explicitly leaves the cost unspecified. The answer also sets per-read cost, since the transformation runs on every read of a protected snippet, and the service must keep serving concurrent requests without one delaying another.

**Recommended:** Option A - The standard library offers a salted key-derivation call that is no more code than a bare digest, so the Simplicity principle does not favour the fast option. The real benefit is not this snippet — anyone holding the storage directory can already read the text unencrypted — but the author's password itself, which people reuse elsewhere; a work factor is what keeps a leaked directory from yielding it.

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| A | Require a deliberately slow salted key-derivation step with a work factor fixed in the spec, accepting a modest added latency (tens of milliseconds) on each read of a protected snippet. Offline guessing stays expensive even for weak passwords. |
| B | Require only a salted one-way transformation with no work factor, keeping protected reads as fast as unprotected ones and relying on the stated threat model: the storage directory's reader is the threat, not an offline cracker. |
| C | Require a slow derivation but leave the work factor to the implementer, constrained only by a stated ceiling on how long a protected read may take. |
| Short | Provide a different short answer (<=5 words) |

You can reply with the option letter (e.g., "A"), accept the recommendation by saying "yes" or "recommended", or provide your own short answer.
